BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A brief upper-level ridge will build into the region Saturday, bringing dry conditions.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Winter Weather Advisory for Harney County OR until 4 AM PST Thursday.
- Winter Weather Advisory for the Camas Prairie from 10 PM MST this evening through 11 AM MST Thursday.
- Cool and unsettled pattern will bring periods of valley rain and accumulating mountain snow through next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Harney County until 4 AM PST Thursday, for an additional 1-3 inches accumulation through the night. The advisory area has also been expanded from northern Harney County to all of Harney County.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A large closed low along West Coast will drift eastward to finish out the week. Southerly flow ahead of the low will continue to transport moisture into SE Oregon and SW Idaho, though entering at the central CA coast isn't the most favorable trajectory for getting deep moisture into our region. This is reflected in the precipitable water values topping out in the 50-60th percentile. Lower elevations will see periods of rain, mainly overnight then again Thursday afternoon/evening. Mountains across SE Oregon and SW Idaho will see fewer breaks in the precipitation as steady southerly flow aloft provides orographic lift. The focus of heavier forecast snowfall remains centered on the southern Boise/Soldier mtns with snow totals of 6-12 inches above 6kft MSL through Friday morning. The heaviest rates will come tonight, and have issued a Winter Weather Advisory for the Camas Prairie to cover the combination of snow and gusty surface winds making for hazardous travel conditions through Thursday morning. Snow levels will increase to 4.5-5.5 kft MSL across the region on Thursday, keeping lower elevations rain. Outside of the Camas, mountain valleys will see lesser amounts (generally 1-3") with mtn amounts in the 3-7" range. Precipitation fills in across lower elevations Thursday afternoon/evening as upper low center tracks through the northern Great Basin. The accompanying dynamics and marginal instability could support heavier banded precipitation across Malheur and Owyhee counties Thursday evening into Thursday night. Models are coming into better agreement with this potential and have trended wetter in these areas which would result in moderate snow amounts south of the Snake River Basin.

Precipitation tapers off from west to east in the valleys on Friday as the low exits the area. Mountains hold onto snow showers through the day, but any additional accumulation will be light (<1"). Winds are gusty again on Friday, but from the northwest in the wake of the low. Temperatures peak on Thursday, pushing a few degrees above normal, then cool back below normal by several degrees on Friday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A brief upper-level ridge will build into the region Saturday, bringing dry conditions. Behind it, a strong upper-level low pressure system will weaken as it moves onshore into the Pacific NW, bringing precipitation chances to the area starting Saturday night into Sunday morning. Precipitation chances will be 30-60% for higher elevations and 10-20% for lower elevations through Monday afternoon. Another brief upper-level ridge will sweep across the area late Monday into early Tuesday before another Pacific system moves in and brings widespread precipitation chances yet again for Wednesday. With these systems moving through, higher elevation precipitation type will be snow, while lower elevations will be more uncertain this far out. Timing of the precipitation will be important, along with any cold pools that remain in lower valleys. The forecast currently reflects this uncertainty, with a wintry mix being the predominant precipitation type. Temperatures will hover near or slightly below normal in SW Idaho and 5-10 degrees below normal in SE Oregon throughout the long term period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Behind the front, conditions are expected to be much cooler. Lows Saturday morning in the plains will drop into the 20s to mid 30s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Gusty winds will continue for portions of the mountains, foothills, and northern plains through the late afternoon.
- Elevated to critical fire weather conditions across portions of the foothills, I-25 corridor, northern plains, and Palmer Divide today.
- Better chances for mountain snow Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Looking at Water Vapor, the upper level shortwave is moving through the area to the east, taking the strongest upper level winds with it. Winds will gradually decrease into the evening, dropping off significantly a little after sunset. We'll see very brief upper level ridging in between our two systems on Thursday. An upper level trough will move onto the northwest coast of the U.S. on Thursday, approaching the area on Friday. A little shortwave will precede the main trough late Thursday into early Friday, bringing snow chances to the mountains during this time. Pacific moisture will move into the higher terrain with this system at low to mid levels, helping with precip chances in the mountains. Moisture will generally remain higher to the west of our area, with the best chances of snow for our CWA in the Park Range.

The main trough will approach the region late Friday, moving through on Saturday. Surface low pressure will develop on the lee side of the mountains ahead of this system. This low will drag a cold front through the area late Friday into early Saturday, bringing much cooler temperatures.

We could briefly sit in the right entrance of the upper level jet Saturday morning. At the same time we'll see broad upper level support ahead of the trough. Unfortunately, moisture throughout the column doesn't look great, but there should be enough for snow showers in the higher terrain and potentially some light showers in the plains as well. Behind the overnight front, a few models are showing weak upslope flow across the southern foothills and Palmer Divide area in the mid to late morning and early afternoon. This could be enough to trigger some shower activity in the southern foothills and Palmer Divide area, potentially extending into the southern metro. Right now, the NBM has a medium chance (30% to 60%) that the southern metro, Palmer, and southern foothills get at least a trace of snow, with very low chances (<10%) that Denver sees more than an inch. For the higher terrain, snow levels will start out around 6000ft, dropping closer to 4000ft by Saturday morning. As mentioned previously, moisture with this event isn't particularly high, so overall accumulation's will be on the lower end, with liquid amounts generally around a few hundredths to a quarter of an inch (with potential for higher amounts in the Park Range).

Behind the front, conditions are expected to be much cooler. Lows Saturday morning in the plains will drop into the 20s to mid 30s. Lows for Sunday into the middle of next week are forecast to be in the teens to mid 20s for the plains with highs only reaching into the 40s each afternoon. Another shortwave trough is forecast to approach the area late Monday into early Tuesday, bringing additional snow chances to the mountains.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Next Pacific storm system is on tap to move across the region through the course of the weekend, bringing mountain snow and cooler temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High winds will continue through the afternoon hours Wednesday with gusts up to 70 MPH. Strong winds and dry conditions will produce conditions favorable for the rapid spread of wildfire.
- Chances for snow showers return to the mountains Thursday night through Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Strong winds continue across the forecast area early this afternoon. All zones that were originally in a High Wind Warning have verified with flying colors. Some of the top gusts so far include Bordeaux with 80 MPH, Quealy Dome with 78 MPH, and Deer Creek hitting 76 MPH. Strong winds have even spread into Nebraska, with a High Wind Warning being issued for the entire panhandle until 5 PM this evening. Some High Wind Warnings have already expired on time, and the remaining Warnings will also expire at 5 PM. Winds will gradually weaken as the afternoon progresses. The upper-level trough responsible for the winds will eject out of the CWA, quickly easing MSLP gradients across the area. As a result, winds will decrease by this evening. The Laramie Range could still see some lingering windiness this evening as 50 kt winds aloft hang over the range through about midnight. The rest of the forecast area will see winds calm overnight with mostly clear skies. This will lead to low temperatures near average.

Fleeting, shallow, upper-level ridging will move into the CWA for Thursday. With it, slightly warmer temperatures and a dry airmass are expected. Highs on Thursday will be anywhere from 5 to 10 degrees warmer than Wednesday, with the biggest temperature increase expected west of the Laramie Range. Highs across most of the CWA will be in the upper 40s to mid 50s. Although dry conditions are expected with low relative humidity across portions of southeast Wyoming, winds will be much calmer for most of the forecast area, so fire weather concerns will not be an issue for Thursday. Locally breezy conditions will be possible in far western Carbon County ahead of the next storm system to move in later Thursday evening. Clouds will increase throughout the day, with snow and the next cold front arriving Thursday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Next Pacific storm system is on tap to move across the region through the course of the weekend, bringing mountain snow and cooler temperatures. The aforementioned system will move into the US as a closed system, but by the time it moves into our neck of the woods should become an open trough. A second, weaker system may drop into the region from Canada and combine with the overall flow on Saturday, with these features then progressing by Sunday as a transient ridge then becomes the dominant feature to start next week. By Tuesday though our next system will move into the region to end the forecast period. For Friday into Saturday we're still on track for some snowfall to move up with the Pacific system, but with the strongest moisture remaining to our south and east alongside the best forcing, the bulk of this activity should be relegated to orographic lift across the mountains, though some light snow overspreading into the nearby lower elevation zones and valleys could be possible, and on Saturday we could even see some precipitation moving into the I-80 corridor from Cheyenne through Sidney. Also on Friday some meager instability will be present west of the Laramie Range which could promote some snow squall activity. Colder temperatures also accompany these systems, and we'll see the warmer than average highs from Thursday and Friday plummeting by Saturday with highs around 5 degrees below normal, placing the region in the 30's to 40's. Sunday we'll dry out under the transient ridge, but by early next week the incoming system brings another chance at widespread precipitation mainly in the form of light snow. But with how precipitation chances have been evaporating as we get within 1 to 3 days of the event, don't be surprised if once again the mountains are the only location to see any noteworthy accumulations by the time we hit next week. Overall there is moderate to high confidence in the forecast with the only true variations in ensembles showing towards the end of the period between the snowfall expectations early next week as well as the strength of the features as we move into the middle of next week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Models agree on this system shifting the storm track/jet stream farther south over eastern Utah and Western Colorado bringing more unsettled weather to the region through the coming Thanksgiving week and possibly beyond.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Temperatures will trend downward Friday and beyond, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.
- The next storm will bring measurable snowfall to the mountains Thursday night into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Models are in good agreement with satellite imagery showing a deep cold low well off the coast of the Pacific Northwest/Northern California starting to make the turn to the east to move inland over Oregon/Northern California this evening into Thursday pushing a well developed active frontal boundary inland ahead of it while the system that went through last night has moved out onto the Northern Plains. The weak transient ridge between these two systems is moving out of the Great Basin into the Rocky Mountains with the lingering showers and clouds across the northern mountains this morning quickly evaporating under the subsidence from the ridge. As the low to the west moves in through the Great Basin Thursday, it transitions into an open wave trough tracking across eastern Utah and Western Colorado Friday into Saturday. Look for the cold front to push through the region overnight Thursday into Friday morning with snow levels dropping to 6000 feet across the northern areas to 7000 feet across the southern areas. As the moisture associated with this system comes through the Pacific Northwest with the Front, there isn't a lot of it available, and thus there won't be major impacts as this system moves through. Expect light to moderate snow showers mostly through the northern and central mountains overnight Thursday into Friday with four to eight inches possible on the western mountain faces and only one to three inches forecast on Rabbit Ears and Vail Passes. There is still a lot of variance in the models, especially on timing of this system moving through, but the worst impacts look to be Friday morning. Even though snow amounts are on the light side, ground/road surface temperatures have cooled. Expect possible icy and/or snowpacked conditions on the higher mountain passes mostly across the northern half of the region. Allow extra time if you will be traveling through these areas Thursday night and Friday.

Models agree on this system shifting the storm track/jet stream farther south over eastern Utah and Western Colorado bringing more unsettled weather to the region through the coming Thanksgiving week and possibly beyond. Expect a disturbance passing through the region every few days with minor impacts to travel mostly through the mountain areas. Stay tuned for updates as the timing of these disturbances is indeterminant beyond the first few days of the forecast. What you can expect is that temperatures will cool about ten degrees Friday and beyond with the daily highs and low about five degrees below the seasonal normal.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Models consistently show the system pushing east of us on Sunday, with cool but mild weather returning through mid-late Monday. Looking further into next week, latest trends hint at another incoming trough bringing more snow to the mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - New system moves in Thurs Night thru Saturday. Strong, gusty winds are expected across the area, with snow over the Continental Divide.
- Heaviest snow expected over the San Juans.
- Cool and mild Sun-Mon, with more active weather expected for the mountains next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Dry and breezy the rest of the day today, with highs in the 50s-60s across the region. Passing shortwave will continue moving off to our northeast, giving us a brief lull between systems. Conditions on Thursday will be similar, dry and mild with high temps just a few degrees lower than today. Clouds will start to increase by the afternoon, and though we'll still see some gusty south winds over the plains and San Luis Valley, gusts should be less frequent a weaker than today's.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Starting Thursday Night, a broad upper trough will move in from the west, giving us increasing southwest flow aloft. Snow will spread into the Continental Divide, accumulating across the peaks of the mountains through Friday and into early Saturday. Latest guidance shows the heaviest accumulations over the San Juans once again, with widespread 2-4 inch amounts, though locally higher amounts to around 6 inches will be possible. Meanwhile, the rest of the Continental Divide is forecasted to get less than 2 inches, with little to no snow for the eastern mountains. Overall, the system is relatively lacking in deep moisture, and QPF estimates have continued to decrease wit the last few sets of model runs, though this could be offset somewhat by orographics.

As the system pushes east into the weekend, a cold front will push through Friday Night into Saturday, bringing colder temperatures to the region as well as rain/snow showers. As of now, scattered showers will move in behind the front over the Palmer Divide and Pikes Peak area. High temperatures for the plains will drop from the 50s-60s on Friday into the 40s to low-50s on Saturday, so even if El Paso County sees some flakes hit the ground, currently no accumulation is expected.

Winds will also be an impact concern with this system, as a strengthening upper jet maximum passes over us on the leading side of the trough. Most of the day on Friday, our CWA will be seeing strong winds out of the southwest. Over the plains, latest NBM shows gusts 35-40 mph, though isolated gusts to 50 mph will be possible. The San Luis Valley seems to be getting the strongest winds Friday afternoon, with gusts 50-55 mph expected. Probabilistic data only shows the potential to hit High Wind criteria in the valley for an hour or two Friday afternoon, with less than half the members, so while no highlights are needed as of right now the model trends will have to be looked at for increases in gust potential.

Models consistently show the system pushing east of us on Sunday, with cool but mild weather returning through mid-late Monday. Looking further into next week, latest trends hint at another incoming trough bringing more snow to the mountains.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: 50% of guidance have another system moving through the state on Monday that could be cold enough for valley snow to accompany the entire event, but the other 50% of guidance do not bring this system through.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A longer duration storm will come through the area in pieces from Thursday morning through Saturday morning with the highest snow totals across the northern mountains and valley snow possible Friday evening into Saturday morning.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The 12Z KSLC sounding showed -11.5C at 700mb which is on the low end of the forecast envelope which is what led to the widespread valley snow yesterday. This has also led to our first freezing temperatures of the season at KSLC which ties the latest on record. Temperatures will remain 3-8 degrees below normal through the next week.

A transient ridge has moved overhead with mostly clear skies and cold temperatures, especially for areas that have snow covering the ground. This will be a short-lived dry period before a broad slow moving trough pushes into the Great Basin tomorrow. This trough will bring several rounds of precipitation through Saturday morning. The first round moves in on Thursday with the heaviest across southern Utah as an atmospheric river rounds the southern periphery of the Sierras coinciding with the left exit region of a 110+ kt jet. Snow levels will start much lower with this system with snow levels generally between 6000-6500 feet. Flow aloft will stay southwesterly during the duration of this first wave which will favor aspects that do well in southerly flow.

This first wave of precipitation associated with the initial trough axis will exit by Friday afternoon. This will likely be the only period of precipitation for the southern half of Utah as the trailing wave Friday night into Saturday morning focuses on northern Utah/SW Wyoming. This limited duration across southern Utah will keep snow totals generally between 4-8" for the southern mountains.

A secondary trailing wave on Friday evening will usher in colder air aloft with median 700 mb temperatures falling to -10C which would be cold enough to bring snow levels down to valley floors by Friday evening as winds aloft become west/northwesterly. Guidance is split on exactly how this will play out. A more westerly flow will favor areas of Weber/Davis county, particularly the benches while a more northwesterly flow will favor Tooele and Salt Lake valleys. Moisture will remain in the mid to lower portions of the column through 00Z Saturday before becoming confined to the lower portion of the column, but this could allow snow to continue through Saturday morning for areas across northern Utah that reside in the preferential flow regime. Snow totals for the northern mountains will range from 10-20" with higher totals across the preferred aspects of 24"+. Valley snow totals will be between 1-4" once a transition from rain to snow occurs.

50% of guidance have another system moving through the state on Monday that could be cold enough for valley snow to accompany the entire event, but the other 50% of guidance do not bring this system through. Regardless, temperatures will be cold with the first freeze of the season likely for portions of Zion and lower Washington county Saturday and Sunday morning.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Recent wind-drifted snow will keep the avalanche danger elevated near and above treeline on slopes facing west through north to east. Small avalanches will be easy to trigger, especially just below ridgelines. Steer clear of steep slopes if you feel wind-stiffened snow or see shooting cracks as you travel.
Below treeline conditions are generally safe due to thin or non-existent snow cover.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Recent winds created pockets of drifted snow at higher elevations. These pockets are isolated but could produce small avalanches. Assess high-elevation steep slopes before committing.
Avalanche danger increases Friday as a storm moves through.
